name: Erythromycin topical

lead: Topical erythromycin is a prescription macrolide antibiotic, most commonly a 2% solution, whose US-labelled indication is acne vulgaris. The payoff is fewer inflamed pimples and clearer skin.

It acts against acne-associated skin bacteria such as Cutibacterium acnes, and reviews of acne treatment list it alongside clindamycin among commonly used topical antimicrobials. Small older reports have also described it used with a topical corticosteroid in perioral dermatitis.

paras: It is applied to the affected skin as a prescribed solution as part of an acne routine, and is often combined with other acne treatments. Improvement is gradual over weeks.

The label lists dryness, peeling, itching, redness and oiliness, and warns that colitis has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents. Human pregnancy data are inadequate. It is prescription only.

angle.text: Topical erythromycin is a long-standing prescription antibiotic for acne. It reduces acne-associated bacteria on the skin, which means fewer inflamed spots and clearer skin; acne is its labelled use.

lead: Topical erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic applied to the skin, most commonly as a 2% solution, whose US-labelled indication is the topical treatment of acne vulgaris.[1] It acts against skin bacteria such as Propionibacterium acnes (now Cutibacterium acnes), and reviews of topical acne antimicrobials list erythromycin alongside clindamycin as commonly used agents.[2]

Beyond acne, small older reports have described erythromycin solution used with a topical corticosteroid in perioral dermatitis.[3] Its label lists local reactions such as peeling, dryness, itching, redness and oiliness, and warns that pseudomembranous colitis has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents.[1]
Little looksmaxxing-community material was found for this entry; it appears in an appearance context because of acne.

paras: The US drug label for erythromycin topical solution 2% lists a single indication, the topical treatment of acne vulgaris.[1] A review of topical clindamycin describes topical antimicrobials as working partly by suppressing propionibacteria and partly through non-antimicrobial mechanisms, and names topical erythromycin among the commonly used agents.[2]
A 1983 report in Cutis described six patients with perioral dermatitis treated with 1.5 percent erythromycin solution together with a tapered hydrocortisone valerate cream.[3]

The label reports occasional local reactions including peeling, dryness, itching, erythema and oiliness, as well as eye irritation and skin tenderness; generalized urticarial reactions requiring systemic steroids have also been reported.[1]

The label carries a warning that pseudomembranous colitis has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, and notes there are no adequate, well-controlled studies in pregnant women, advising use in pregnancy only if clearly needed.[1]

A review of topical clindamycin in acne reported that clindamycin appears superior in efficacy to some other options, and treats erythromycin as one of several accepted topical antimicrobials.[2] A 1983 case series of six perioral dermatitis patients reported success with erythromycin solution plus hydrocortisone valerate; it was not a controlled trial.[3]
A Phase 4 trial comparing the anti-inflammatory effects of topical erythromycin and clindamycin in acne patients (30 participants) is registered as recruiting.[4]
